`baseball_player_stats` carries **no unique constraint** on that tuple — only the primary key on `id`. Nothing downstream would have caught the duplicate, and duplicated stats feed averages, leaderboards and CoachHelm.

That check mattered: **three earlier fail-open candidates tonight turned out to be backstopped by real constraints and were left alone.** This one is not, so it is a real defect rather than a pattern match.

## The fix

The row is skipped and counted as a create-conflict rather than guessed at — the coach sees an honest per-row failure instead of a silent double-write. Fourth genuine fail-open of the night, and the second that corrupts data rather than misleading someone.

## #1324 and #1325 merged, then #1326 undid them

#1326's diff should have been the genome page plus the genome loader. It also rewrote **four files it had no business touching**, net **-161 lines**:

| file | what came back |
|---|---|
| `team/page.tsx` | the silent redirect off Team Info |
| `roster/[id]/page.tsx` | 404s a player who **is** on the coach's roster |
| `qualifiers/[id]/page.tsx` | 404s the qualifier; field renders with no scores |
| `rounds/[id]/page.tsx` | 404s an existing round; coach access check back to failing closed **in silence** |

## Cause

I branched `fix/genome-page-read-failures` off `origin/main` **before** those two merged, and my push tool builds its commit from `origin/main..HEAD` with `base_tree: origin/main` — using a possibly-stale local ref. The branch therefore carried stale copies of files it had never edited, and merging it reverted them.

**"PR merged" was not the same as "fix is in main", and I had been treating those as identical all day.** Three PRs reported as shipped were not.

Restored from the squash commits that introduced them (`09b0cfd32`, `8c1e8ee1b`). #1326's genome work is verified still present — that fix is not being undone in turn.

## The ratchet did not catch this, and that's worth knowing

The revert took the count from 1098 back to **1104**, still under the **1107** baseline — so it read as *no regression*. **A ratchet only sees the number rising; it cannot see fixes disappearing underneath a loose baseline.**

Baseline is tightened to the true **1098** here, which closes the slack for these six reads.

## Recurrence prevented

The push tool now fetches `origin/main` and **refuses to push a branch that isn't on top of it**, naming the reversion risk. It would have blocked #1326.

## Correction first

An earlier revision of this PR claimed **Vercel Skew Protection is not enabled**. That was wrong.

I read the setting with an **unauthenticated** API call. It returned `403`, my parser did `.get("skewProtectionMaxAge", "(absent)")` on the error body, and printed `"(absent)"`. A permissions failure rendered as a fact about configuration — the exact false-zero shape this entire day has been about, committed by me while fixing it elsewhere.

Authenticated: `skewProtectionMaxAge = 604800`. **It is on, 7-day window, Pro plan.**

## What that changes

Deployment skew is therefore a poor explanation for the 17:35 login error, and this PR no longer asserts it. **The cause is not established.** Candidates that produce the same message:

- a service worker answering the action POST with an HTML document
- the action returning a non-RSC response (a 500 page, a middleware redirect)

## What still stands

*"An unexpected response was received from the server"* is Next's message for a Server Action response it could not parse. It is **not** a login failure — nothing is wrong with the account or password — but the screen said *"An unexpected error occurred. Please try again."*, and pressing the same button reproduces it.

Seen in production 2026-08-07 17:35: a Guilford player on the iOS app, on a page load with `transferSize: 0` (entirely from cache).

Whatever produced it, **the client is holding something it cannot use, and one reload replaces it.** That's true without knowing the cause, which is why the recovery is kept while the diagnosis is reopened.

- Reloads **once**, guarded by `sessionStorage` rather than component state — the reload destroys state, so a component-state guard would loop the sign-in screen on a genuinely broken deploy.
- Storage unavailable (private mode) fails **closed**: no reload, show the message.
- Logs at `low`, not `high`.

body:
## What a real player saw today

At **17:39**, Sawyer Slate (Guilford) retried a schedule-image import **three times in fifty seconds**. The app told him:

> the upstream provider account is rate-limiting requests. **This clears on its own**; the request was not lost.

The Anthropic account had been out of credit since that morning. Waiting could never have worked. He was told to wait by a promise the code had no basis for making.

## The fix

A `429` does **not** distinguish a throttled-but-healthy account from one that has run out of credit — providers use it for both, and without a message body the two are identical. The recovery promise is gone.

"The request was not lost" is true and stays. The copy now names out-of-credit as the likelier cause when it keeps happening.

## Why I couldn't tell which it was

Unlike the sibling call sites in `golf.ts` and `compose.ts`, `schedule-image.ts` recorded `providerFaultKind` and `provider` but **not** `providerMessage`. The stored record reads provider `"unknown"` with an empty message — the evidence needed to tell a throttle from an exhaustion had been discarded at the one call site that needed it.

That's recorded now, so the next occurrence is diagnosable instead of ambiguous.

## Tests

**Verified non-vacuous:** both copy tests fail against the previous string and pass after.

A third test pins that an explicit `"credit balance is too low"` still classifies as `credit_exhausted` rather than `rate_limited` — this change must not blur the two, since those two faults have opposite advice.

## The business bottom line

This is the **second** real user hit today from the same billing state: CoachHelm chat at 14:54, schedule import at 17:39. The code no longer lies about it, but the account still needs topping up.

`bulkCheckIn` scopes writes to active members of the event's team, so an empty result **correctly denies everyone** — that behaviour is kept, since a scoping read that couldn't run must never widen access.

What was wrong is what a **failed** read then reported: `success: true` with every player counted as a failure. To the coach that reads as *"none of these players are on your team"*, when the truth is that we could not check.

A coach checking in the squad before a match sees nobody check in, with no reason given. Attendance records carry eligibility and discipline weight, so a silent zero there is not cosmetic.

body:
Found by the ratchet shipped in #1327, then verified by hand.

## 1. A task assigned to nobody

`createTaskFromTemplate` resolved "all players" **after** creating the task, and discarded the roster read's error. An empty `playerIds` then skipped the `playerIds.length > 0` assignment guard and the action returned **success**.

So a coach applies a compliance template to the whole team, sees it succeed, and the task sits assigned to nobody. **Identical defect, identical shape, to the announcements roster read** fixed earlier today — which is the point: this is one bug class, not a series of unrelated ones.

The roster is now resolved **before** the insert, so a failure costs nothing: nothing is created, and the message says so.

## 2. A rostered player told they aren't assigned

`completeTask`'s membership check needed more care, because `.single()` reports "no such row" as **PGRST116 rather than null data** — the two cases have to be told apart explicitly rather than lumped together.

Discarding the error meant any read failure told a player who **is** on the team that they are not assigned to this task, and threw their completion away.

## Tests

**Verified non-vacuous:** the roster-failure test fails against the previous `tasks.ts` and passes after. The happy-path test passes in *both* — that one is the guard against over-correcting until normal use starts erroring, which is the real risk with this kind of fix.

## Note on scope

This clears 2 of the 25 unchecked reads in `tasks.ts`. The other 23 are coach/team/task authorization lookups of the form "read failed → tell the user their profile doesn't exist". Same class, lower blast radius, and not worth bundling into a fix that touches write ordering. The ratchet keeps the count from growing while they're paid down.

body:
## The finding

Today's code-red was dominated by **one** root cause. `supabase-js` **resolves** database errors as `{ data: null, error }` rather than throwing, so:

```ts
const { data } = await supabase.from(...).select(...)
```

turns a read that **failed** into a read that **found nothing** — and the UI then states that nothing as fact.

I fixed 15 instances across 12 files today. **This rule finds 1,111 call sites.** I fixed about 1.4% of them, which settles the question of whether manual sweeping would ever converge.

| area | count |
|---|---|
| `app/golf/actions` | 474 |
| `app/baseball/actions` | 227 |
| `lib/baseball/read-models` | 50 |
| `app/golf/(dashboard)` | 40 |
| `app/baseball/(dashboard)` | 37 |
| `lib/coachhelm/v3` | 31 |

Not all 1,111 are bugs — plenty are internal paths where emptiness is never shown to anyone. But every user-facing one I checked today *was*.

## Why the rule is registered but `"off"`

**`npm run lint` runs with `--max-warnings 0` and is a hard CI gate, and `.lint-baseline.json` is `{}` — the repo is genuinely lint-zero.** Switching this rule on globally would fail the Lint job on **every PR in the repo**. How much of that debt to service, and when, is your call, not something to slip in attached to a bug fix.

`npm run lint` still exits 0. Verified, not assumed.

## What enforces it instead

A ratchet: `npm run audit:supabase-errors` counts violations and fails **only if the number goes up**. New code cannot add an unchecked read; the existing 1,111 get paid down directory by directory, lowering the baseline as they go. At 0, flip the rule to `"warn"` and delete the script.

## Verified rather than assumed

- The rule flags both real bug shapes and **neither** correct form (`error` bound, or the whole result kept for `result.error`).
- Injecting one new unchecked read moves 1111 → 1112 and the script exits **1**; removing it exits **0**.
- I checked those exit codes **directly, not through a pipe** — `node script | tail` reports *tail's* status, which would have made this gate silently useless while looking like it worked.
- A count of 0 is treated as a **broken audit**, not a clean repo, since that far more likely means the rule failed to load than that 1,000 call sites got fixed.

## Not wired into CI

Deliberately. Adding `npm run audit:supabase-errors` to `ci.yml` is a one-line change whenever you want to start enforcing it.

The same failed-read-as-empty class, now on the dashboard **pages**. Each one wears a different mask, which is why each reads to a user like a different broken feature.

## 1. Team Info — a silent redirect

Four reads on the player branch of `/dashboard/team` discarded their errors. A failed membership or team read is indistinguishable from "this player has no team", so the player was **bounced to the dashboard with no message at all**.

That's worse than a wrong message: nothing to report, nothing to retry, and the Team tab just appears not to work. Combined with the roster page telling the same player *"You haven't joined a team yet"*, a transient DB blip could convincingly impersonate having been cut from the squad.

The roster read gets the same treatment — unread renders as a team with nobody on it, which reads as "everyone got removed". The staff read stays non-fatal (it only hides the head coach's name) but now logs, because "no coach listed" is exactly what F031 was raised about.

**The redirect is unchanged for a player who genuinely has no team.**

## 2. Detail pages — a 404

On a detail page the mask is `notFound()`: a 404 for a record the coach just clicked.

- `roster/[id]` — the membership read is the likelier of the two to fire, and it 404s a player who **is** on the roster the coach opened them from.
- `qualifiers/[id]` — same for the qualifier itself. Its **rounds** read is the worse one, and it's the identical defect fixed in the leaderboard *action* (#1320) sitting here in the coach's detail *page*: the per-player breakdown is built from those rows, so a failed read doesn't blank the page — it renders the full field with no scores against anybody. Coaches pick travel squads off that screen.

Absent and unreadable are not the same answer, and only the first is a 404. Both now log the real cause and throw, landing on the route error boundary with its retry. **`notFound()` is untouched for records that genuinely don't exist.**

Three more instances of the same class: a failed database read rendering as a confident "there is nothing here".

## 1. The roster told players on a team that they had no team

The **coach** branch of `/dashboard/roster` checks both of its reads for errors. The **player** branch checked neither. When the membership read failed — a transient RLS denial, a timeout — it fell straight through to:

> **No Team Found**
> You haven't joined a team yet. Ask your coach for a join code.

...shown to a player who **is** on the roster. This is very likely a chunk of what got reported as "teams joining doesn't work": the join succeeded, the roster page just couldn't read, blamed the player, and sent them to their coach for a code they didn't need.

The teammate read one step further in had the same trap — unread renders as a team of one.

Both now log the real cause and say we couldn't load it, matching what the coach branch a hundred lines below already does. **"No Team Found" is unchanged for a player who genuinely has no team.**

## 2. Course library — the strict loader didn't keep its own promise

Its docstring says it exists so a failure "can't masquerade as *this team has saved nothing yet*". That guarantee covered only the **first** of its two reads. The second resolves each saved row's course, and the mapper drops any row whose course is missing — so a failed courses read emptied the map, filtered out every row, and rendered exactly the empty library the strict variant was written to prevent. It now throws there too.

The lenient sibling stays lenient (it feeds the picker's Saved tab, where a degraded tab beats a broken picker) but now **logs** instead of silently reporting "you haven't saved any courses".

## 3. Task reminders — not knowing who you are is not "nothing is due"

The coach and player id lookups discarded their errors, and a null id isn't neutral in the filter they feed: it fails every clause. One failed lookup silently dropped **every** reminder the user had and returned an empty list with no error — while the reminders read itself, which *is* error-checked, made the query look healthy. The assignment lookup below it had the same trap for players.

## Tests

5 cases in `src/test/golf/actions/read-failure-vs-empty-batch2.test.ts`. **Verified non-vacuous: 3 fail against the previous code, all 5 pass after.**

The two that pass in *both* are deliberate over-correction guards — the failure mode of this kind of fix is tightening until healthy empty states start erroring. A genuinely empty library still reads as empty, and a user who is neither coach nor player still gets a clean empty list rather than an error.

## The bug

This file's docstring already stated the right contract:

> Returns honest empty arrays on a genuinely-empty team, never fabricated data; **a real DB/network failure is allowed to throw** (the route's error.tsx / retry boundary is the correct place to surface that).

The code never met it. `supabase-js` **resolves** database errors as `{ data: null, error }` instead of throwing, so three legs of the `Promise.all` turned a failed read into an empty one and the boundary never fired:

- **events** (`get_player_hub_events`) — the player was shown "no upcoming events", **mandatory ones included**, and could no-show;
- **travel** — the itinerary carrying the departure time and location simply wasn't there;
- **tasks** — assigned work, including upload-compliance items, vanished.

None of the three logged anything.

The **announcements** leg in the *same function* already tracks its failure via `announcementsLoadError`. That's what makes these three an oversight rather than a decision.

## The fix

All three now log the real cause and throw — which is what the docstring said should happen.

I checked the caller before doing this: `redirectToLoginOnExpiredSession` redirects only on the exact message `'Not authenticated'` (the narrow token-refresh race) and re-raises everything else. So this lands on the route error boundary with its retry — it does **not** bounce the player to login.

## Tests

body:
## The bug

"Send this to the whole team" is decided by one read of `golf_team_members`, and that read discarded its error and returned `[]`.

Empty is the single most dangerous value it can return, because every guard downstream is written as `targetPlayerIds.length > 0`. So a roster read that **failed** did not fail — it quietly meant *send to nobody*:

- the announcement row was created,
- its inline tasks were created and assigned to **no one**,
- the email and push fan-out was skipped,
- and the action returned `success`.

A coach publishing a mandatory waiver saw a success toast while zero players received it. Nothing was logged either — which is the tell, because the sibling `users` read a few lines below in the *same function* already handles its failure properly. This one was just missed.

The same helper was also read a second time to validate hand-picked recipients, where a failure emptied the set and made every selected player "not on your team" — accusing the coach of picking the wrong players when the truth was that we could not check.

## The fix

The roster is read **once**, and **before anything is written**. A failure now costs nothing: the action returns and no announcement exists. The message says nothing was sent, because nothing was.

## What this deliberately does not fix

The same helper feeds the acknowledgement-progress **denominator** in two read paths (`getAnnouncements`, `getAnnouncementById`). Those still return `0` on failure — wrong in a visible way (a real numerator over zero) rather than a plausible one — but they now **log** it instead of failing in silence.

Making them honest means typing the count `number | null` and teaching the progress UI to render "unknown". That's a UI change and is not bundled here.

## Tests

`src/test/golf/actions/announcement-roster-read-failure.test.ts` — fails closed and writes nothing on a failed roster read; does not accuse the coach when the check couldn't run; still publishes normally when the read succeeds.

**Verified non-vacuous:** 2 of the 3 fail against the previous `announcements.ts`; all 3 pass after.

body:
## The bug

`supabase-js` **resolves** database errors as `{ data: null, error }` rather than throwing, so `const { data } = await …` quietly turns a read that *failed* into a read that *found nothing*. Four reads on the qualifier leaderboard path discarded their error that way.

In increasing order of damage:

| Read | What a failure looked like to the user |
|---|---|
| qualifier | "Qualifier not found" — sends a coach looking for data loss that never happened. Only `PGRST116` actually means no rows. |
| player lookup | `isPlayerEntered` recomputed against a player id we never learned → an entered player is told they haven't entered, and offered the Enter button again |
| entries | early return answers `success: true, leaderboard: []` — byte-identical to a qualifier nobody has entered — so an RLS denial renders as "no entries yet" on a full field |
| rounds | **the worst.** Every consumer reads `rounds \|\| []`, so a failed read doesn't blank the page: it produces a complete, confident leaderboard on which nobody has posted a score |

That last one is the reason this isn't cosmetic. Coaches pick travel squads off that screen, and a scoreless-but-confident leaderboard is indistinguishable from a real one.

## The fix

Each read now separates "we could not read this" from "there is nothing here", logs the real cause with a stable action name, and says so in the copy.

The cheap version of this fix breaks coaches, so that case is pinned explicitly: **a coach with no `golf_players` row is still not an error** — that null is expected, they still see the board.

## Tests

`src/test/golf/actions/qualifier-leaderboard-failure-vs-empty.test.ts`, 7 cases covering each read's failure, the genuinely-empty field, the coach-with-no-player-row case, and PGRST116-vs-real-failure.

**Verified non-vacuous:** 4 of the 7 fail against the previous `golf.ts`; all 7 pass after. (Assertions match on logged content rather than call counts, because `withAdminObserved` also logs any `success: false` return — counting would have pinned the wrapper, not this action.)

body:
## What this changes

`/api/inngest` reports a signed request that fails signature validation. The SDK's 401 carries no reason, and it rejects for two unrelated causes:

- the signature is older than five minutes → **clock skew**
- the HMAC doesn't match → **wrong key**

The route asserted the second one unconditionally. A latency blip would have sent someone to rotate a credential that was never the problem. The `t=` half of `x-inngest-signature` is a plain unix timestamp and needs no secret to read, so the two are now told apart by measurement, against the SDK's own five-minute tolerance (`RequestSignature.hasExpired`, inngest@4).

## Why the key-mismatch message got longer

It's the message someone acts on, so it now carries the evidence rather than a conclusion:

- These 401s land **within seconds of every production deploy** — 10:52:26/10:52:30 and 11:52:29/11:52:31, each pair straddling a `Deployed …` event. That is Inngest Cloud re-syncing, not a scanner.
- The **event key from the same pair is rejected too**: every round submitted since 2026-07-30 logged `Inngest API Error: 404 Event key not found` (real users, `clynde@guilford.edu` and `lane4275@gmail.com`).
- Both values are **well-formed and not swapped** — `signkey-prod-<64 hex>` and an 86-char event key, neither padded, checked without printing either.

Two independent, correctly-shaped credentials both rejected means they belong to an Inngest app or environment that no longer recognises them. So the named fix is "copy the current keys from the app that is syncing, or delete the manual overrides and let the Inngest↔Vercel integration manage them, then redeploy" — not "reissue the signing key".

**This still needs Nick**: no code change can make Inngest accept a credential it doesn't have. Rounds are unaffected (the inline fallback runs), but they run without retry or crash recovery.

## Also verified while here

inngest@4 returns 401 for an **unsigned GET in cloud mode** (`handleAction`, `method === "GET"` → `unauthorizedResponse`). The unsigned short-circuit shipped in #1316 is therefore byte-identical to SDK behaviour and does **not** block Inngest's introspection — a regression I went looking for and did not find.

## Tests

`src/test/api/inngest-signature-diagnosis.test.ts` — 4 cases: unsigned probe is answered 401 without waking the SDK and without logging; a 600s-old signature blames the clock and explicitly says *do not reissue*; a 2s-old signature blames the key; an accepted request says nothing.

Found by testing **dual-team RLS visibility** on Shenandoah, which runs a Men's and a Women's squad under one organization with one coach staffing both.

`createConversation` stamps `team_id` from the **creator's resolved active team**, not from the participants. On a two-squad program that's frequently the *other* squad — in production, a 1:1 DM between two **Women's** players carries the **Men's** `team_id`.

The participants policy then granted self-join to anyone on "the conversation's team", so a **Men's player could insert himself into that DM and read it.** Reproduced on production; it returned 0 messages only because that particular DM is empty, so the mechanism is the finding, not the payload.

**This is partly a consequence of the tenant binding I added earlier today.** That gate trusts `conversation.team_id` — which is exactly the field a two-squad program gets wrong. It closed the cross-**org** hole and left a cross-**squad** one.

## The fix

That gate exists for the **team chat** bootstrap — letting a member join their squad's group chat. It was never meant to cover private DMs, where the only person who should add participants is the creator.

Self-add now requires **either**:
- you **created** the conversation (a definer check, because `golf_conversations` SELECT denies a brand-new row — this is the bootstrap DM creation depends on), **or**
- it is a **team chat** on a team you belong to.

## Verified on production — attack and controls

```
ATTACK   men's player self-joins women's DM ..... BLOCKED 42501
CONTROL  coach creates DM, self+other, posts .... PASSES
CONTROL  player creates DM to their coach ....... PASSES
CONTROL  coach still sees women's roster (6) .... PASSES
```

**Everything else in the dual-squad matrix was already correct:** across teams, rosters, calendar events, classes and announcements, each player sees only their own squad and the coach sees both.

Deliberately not changed: the misfiled `team_id` on that DM. With this policy a DM's `team_id` no longer grants access, so it's cosmetic — and re-stamping historical rows would be a guess about which squad a two-squad conversation "belongs" to.

Follow-up to #1315, **which did not work.**

I verified that against production rather than assuming it had: after deploying, the same unauthenticated `curl` still produced all three Sentry groups at `14:55:02Z` — and the stack trace showed my own wrapper in it, so the code was live and simply ineffective.

**The reason:** the Inngest SDK *catches* its own signature failure, reports it, and returns 401 itself. It never throws. An outer `try/catch` therefore never sees anything, which is why wrapping the handler changed nothing.

The only place to stop it is **before delegating**. An unsigned request now returns 401 without the SDK ever running.

The response is byte-identical to what the SDK already returned for an unsigned request (`401` + `{"message":"Unauthorized"}`), so nothing about Inngest's own behaviour changes — real traffic from Inngest Cloud always carries `x-inngest-signature` and still reaches the SDK untouched.

A **signed** request that fails is still reported once, naming the fix, because that one means the key genuinely no longer matches and durable jobs are degraded.

Typecheck and lint clean.

body:
## Root cause — proven, not inferred

`/api/inngest` is a **public URL**. Any request without an Inngest signature — a port scanner, an uptime check, a crawler, a developer with curl — made the SDK throw, and **one** such request produced **three** Sentry groups:

```
Signature validation failed
Error: No x-inngest-signature provided   (or "Error: Invalid signature")
[object Object]                          with the body "MESSAGE LOST"
```

The third is unreadable because the SDK reports a bare `{ method: 'GET' }`, and `String({ method: 'GET' })` is `[object Object]`. Three entries sat at the top of the Bridge incident queue, none naming a cause, all reading **"0 users"** — because there is no user; it's a robot.

**I proved this rather than reasoning about it:** a single unauthenticated `curl` of the endpoint at `2026-08-07T14:03:10Z` reproduced all three groups exactly. That also explains the two facts that made it look like a key problem — the burst on every deploy (a deploy invites a fresh round of probes), and the 2026-08-06 20:42 start, when the route first went live.

**It is not the signing key.** My earlier read that a 401 proved a bad key was wrong: an unauthenticated GET returning 401 is *correct* behaviour, and the 401 I measured was my own unsigned request.

## What changes

Unsigned requests get the quiet 401 they always deserved, without touching the error pipeline.

A request that **does** carry a signature and still fails is a different thing — that would mean `INNGEST_SIGNING_KEY` no longer matches the Inngest app, silently degrading durable jobs — and it's still reported, once, naming the fix. **Nothing real is suppressed.**

## Also: aborted avatar uploads

There's no `AbortSignal.timeout` in that path, so "Fetch is aborted" can only mean the request was cut off from outside — the user navigated away or picked a different file. It was logged at `high`, so wandering off mid-upload opened a high-severity incident with a red banner. Now `low`, with copy telling the user how to retry.

The global transient-network matcher still deliberately excludes `AbortError` — that reasoning (aborts are our own timeouts firing, a budget worth knowing about) is sound and **untouched**; it simply doesn't apply to a call site that sets no timeout.

Typecheck, lint, 4958 tests pass.

## The defect

`syncClassToCalendar` stamped every occurrence in a series with **one** UTC offset, captured at save time. A semester crosses a daylight-saving boundary, so a schedule entered in August (EDT, −04:00) wrote its November and December occurrences as −04:00 too — and those months are EST. Every meeting after the change was stored an hour early.

**This was not hypothetical and not waiting for November.** It was already wrong in the data: of **879** class events in production, **281 were an hour early**, spanning 2026-11-02 → 2026-12-15, across **17 classes and 2 real teams**. A player looking at their December schedule today saw the wrong time.

## The code fix

`timezone` (IANA, e.g. `America/New_York`) now travels with the sync payload, and the offset is resolved **per occurrence** from it rather than once for the series. A fixed offset simply cannot express "same wall-clock time across a DST change" — only a zone can. `timezoneOffset` remains the fallback for callers not yet updated, and an unrecognised zone falls back rather than guessing.

## The data repair (already applied; tracked in the two migrations here)

It does **not** assume a uniform +1h shift. It recomputes each event from the **class's own wall-clock time**, in the team's timezone, on that event's own local date — correct on either side of the change, and a no-op for the 598 rows that were already right.

A second, smaller repair follows: the first was scoped to rows whose **start** disagreed (exactly the DST population), so it skipped one row whose start was correct but whose **end** was not — `PSY-222-F2F1`, ending 15:00 while its class says 15:30, a stale occurrence whose end never followed an edit. Both are idempotent.

**Verified after: 879 class events, 0 wrong start times, 0 wrong end times.**

## Test

`src/test/lib/class-sync-dst.test.ts` pins that an 08:30 class reads 08:30 in August, November **and** December — and includes a non-vacuity case that reproduces the old single-offset behaviour and asserts it drifts to 07:30, so the suite cannot pass against an implementation that changed nothing.

Typecheck, lint, 1247 tests pass.

From an audit of every GolfHelm surface a **Shenandoah** coach or player sees today. Both new teams are almost entirely empty in production — **0 rounds, 0 qualifiers, 0 announcements, 0 tasks, 0 documents, 0 insights** — so nearly every screen they open is an empty state. **Most were already excellent.** Three were not.

## 1. A failed team lookup told a paying coach they have no team

`dashboard-data.ts` read `teamResult.data` and never its `.error`. supabase-js *resolves* rather than rejects on a DB error, so a timeout or lock wait left `team` null — and `FairwayCoachDashboard` renders the **"Create or join a team"** onboarding funnel when team is null. A coach with a live 9-player roster would be told their program doesn't exist, and pointed at a destructive next action.

This is the worst member of the family: not a wrong number, but a wrong answer to *"does my team exist"*.

`page.tsx` already documents the intended contract — *"a real DB/network outage must SURFACE ... letting this throw only fires on a true failure"* — and relies on this action throwing. It didn't. Now it does, **except for PGRST116**, which is what `.single()` returns when the row genuinely is gone; for that case the onboarding funnel *is* the right screen.

## 2. The flag I added in #1307 was never read

`teamStatsUnavailable` was computed, put on the payload, threaded to the component boundary — then **dropped**. Zero references in the render body. So a failed rounds read still showed "No rounds logged yet", "Trend appears as rounds build" and "No leaderboard yet" to a team with a full season on file.

Computing a flag and not consuming it is the same defect as not computing it; it just looks fixed. Recent Rounds, Performance Trend and Top Performers now each say the read failed.

## 3. "Roster's covered" was an all-clear built on no data

`RosterHealthHeader` branched only on roster size, so 9 players with 0 rounds got *"Roster's covered — everyone with rounds has a focus area and no one's trending down."* Vacuously true — "everyone with rounds" is nobody — and it reads as an assurance the squad has been assessed. **It was the first thing both new Shenandoah coaches saw.**

Now: *"Nothing to assess yet — attention flags appear once players start logging rounds"*, with an em-dash instead of a `0`, because zero reads as a measured result and this is the absence of measurement.

## Test correction

`handles null team gracefully` mocked a not-found error with **no code**, which no real PostgREST response looks like — and that shape is now the signal for an infrastructure fault. It now uses `PGRST116` (what `.single()` actually returns), and a new sibling test pins that a `57014` timeout **throws** rather than rendering the onboarding funnel.

`count || 0` maps the error channel onto the empty-result value — on a failed read `count` is null, so a fault renders as "no unread messages". Four headline tiles and every derived KPI collapsed the PostgREST error channel into the same value as a legitimately empty result — `.count || 0`, `.data || []`, with `.error` never read on any of **six** reads. The action still returned `{success: true}`, so the caller had no signal.

Either makes one count return 55P03/57014 while the gate RPC, reading an untouched table, succeeds.

- `teamStatsUnavailable` mirrors `todayScheduleError`, covering the roster fetch **and both round fetches** — the two the original finding missed (`fetchAllRowsResult` does return the error; `captureIfDenial` only handles RLS denials, so a lock/timeout was returned then dropped)

- Roster tile renders the existing `empty` silhouette instead of `0`, and the invite / roster-full notices no longer fire on an **unknown** roster size — that would have told a coach with a full squad to go recruit

C16 from `docs/the-claude-session-who-wasnt-smart-enough.md`, scoped per the verifier.

The calendar page resolved the player's team inside a try/catch whose **own comment** says rendering an empty calendar *"is indistinguishable from 'my season got wiped'"*. That catch was **dead for the channel it guarded**: supabase-js does not reject on a database error, it resolves with `{ data: null, error }` — and only `.data` was destructured.

A statement timeout, pool exhaustion or PostgREST 5xx fell past the catch, `teamId` became null, the whole events block was skipped, and the player saw an empty season with no error and no retry — **while the shell above still printed their team name**, because the layout runs its own separate query. `revalidate = 30` then cached the empty render, so the swallow actively prolonged it.

The same file already applies the correct pattern to the events fetch 85 lines lower (`if (eventsResult.error) throw`). This applies it to the read that *gates* that fetch. The check sits **after** the try/catch so the catch can't swallow its own throw and double-log.

## Also: the two reads disagreed

The page read **any** membership; the layout reads `status = 'active'`. That asymmetry produced the worst presentation — right team name in the header, empty season beneath — and it removes a latent `maybeSingle` cardinality fault (a transferred player with an old inactive row + a new active one matches two rows → client-side PGRST116). Not firing today (all 69 rows active), but the identical swallow on the identical table **was** a live bug in the join flow.

## The layout logs rather than throws — deliberately

That layout wraps *every* dashboard route, so throwing there would turn a transient blip into a whole-product outage. Logging makes it visible without that blast radius. The calendar page can fail alone, so it throws and gets its error boundary.

## Verifier corrections respected

- **RLS denial is not this channel** — a filtered SELECT returns zero rows and no error.
- **The multi-row case is latent, not live.**

Neither claim is repeated in the code comments.

A pre-check can't catch the other reachable causes (already on a different team, a failed membership read, an RPC error mid-flight). `joinedTeam` is now threaded into the completion step:
- copy says the profile saved but the team join did not

A new user who clicks a coach's team-invite or staff-invite link is sent to `/baseball/signup?returnTo=/baseball/join/CODE`. Both onboarding pages read `baseball_signup_returnTo` at the end and redirect there.

**Nothing ever wrote that key.** The only reference in the whole codebase was a `removeItem` in the signup handler — so the value was never set, and the one line that touched it *deleted* it one step before its only reader. Every first-time signup from an invite link finished onboarding on the generic dashboard, on no team, and had to find and re-open the original link to actually join.

This is the primary self-serve acquisition path: a coach shares a link and expects the player to end up on the roster.

Both halves fixed — the signup form now stores `returnTo` (mirroring `baseball-sign-in-form.tsx`, which has always had this), and the premature removal is gone.

## Why this isn't a two-line change

Making the value actually flow turns a dead branch into a live one, and the **player** onboarding page pushed it straight to `router.push` with no validation — an open redirect from a query string. It now applies the same origin guard the coach onboarding page already had.

Fixing the feature without that would have shipped a redirect vulnerability alongside it.

Two adversarially-confirmed customer-facing defects (C2 and C3 in `docs/the-claude-session-who-wasnt-smart-enough.md`).

## C2 — the Settings "Join a Team" form could never succeed

`createTeamJoinRequest` resolved the code with a direct `.eq('join_code', …)` on `golf_teams`. The only non-admin SELECT policy there is `is_golf_team_coach(id) OR is_golf_team_player(id)` — RLS filters on rows you already belong to, not on the literal you searched for — so the read is **unsatisfiable by construction** for the one population the feature serves. A player typing the correct code was told "Invalid team code" every time, and no request reached the coach. Live since 2026-08-03 (migration `20260803120200` dropped the permissive policy and moved resolution into `golf_team_by_join_code`; every sibling call site was migrated, this one was missed).

Now uses the same definer RPC, and separates a failed **lookup** from a bad **code** so infrastructure faults are never reported to the user as a typo.

**Fixing only that would have turned a dead form into a crashing Settings page.** `getPlayerJoinRequests` embedded `team:golf_teams(...)`, RLS-blind identically, and an `as unknown as` cast asserted non-null while the value was always null for a pending requester — the UI renders `request.team.name`. So both reads are fixed together: new SECURITY DEFINER RPC `golf_my_join_requests` (scoped internally by `golf_players.user_id = auth.uid()`), `team` typed NULLABLE end to end, component optional-chains it.

## C3 — onboarding was erasing every player's email

`completePlayerOnboarding` built the full column set, coerced absent optional fields to `null`, and applied it as an UPDATE. The onboarding page never sends email or phone, so completing onboarding wrote NULL over the address `ensurePlayerRecord` had copied from the auth account minutes earlier.

Measured: **22 of 22 August signups had no email** (April: 10 of 10 populated). Coaches' rosters select `email`, so the entire current cohort — UNC Wilmington and both Shenandoah squads — showed a blank contact column.

Absent optional fields are now omitted rather than nulled; email falls back to the signed-in account's own address.

## Production repair already applied

Migration `backfill_golf_players_email_from_auth` restored the 57 destroyed addresses from `auth.users` (fills NULLs only, never overwrites). **All 82 golf players now have an email; every roster is 100% contactable.**

Also applied to prod: `golf_my_join_requests` (this PR's RPC) and `golf_conversation_participants_tenant_isolation` (the C1 cross-tenant breach — see that finding).

## Tests

The RLS-denial harness already existed and already denied `golf_teams` reads — it was simply never pointed at these two functions, which is why the suite stayed green throughout the outage. It now drives both, including the "lookup failed ≠ bad code" distinction and the null-team render path. Typecheck clean; 512/512 golf action tests pass.

Eight commits closing the Helm Bridge audit. Every production number below was measured against the live database, not estimated.

## The one that mattered most

**Every golf team read 0 errors.** Not most — every one. `admin_events.team_id` is written on 7 of 1,116 weekly error rows and on **zero** error-severity rows, yet all three surfaces that show a team's weekly error count keyed on it alone.

| team | Bridge showed | actual |
|---|---|---|
| Demo University Golf | 0 | 11 |
| Guilford College Men's | 0 | 9 |
| Shenandoah Women's | 0 | 9 |
| Shenandoah University | 0 | 3 |

`TeamHealthTable` paints its green "leader" wash on `health === 'active' && errors7d === 0`, so the board badged the three worst teams as its cleanest, `computeTeamGrade` handed them an **A**, and `sortTeamsByHealth`'s red-first ordering had nothing to sort on.

`resolveTeamErrorCounts` (`data/team-scope.ts`) generalises the union `team-detail.ts` already ran correctly — team_id **OR** the team's resolved roster/staff user ids, incident severities only, auth noise excluded — to many teams in a fixed 6 queries. Counting is into a per-team `Set` of event ids, so a row carrying both attributions counts once while a user on two teams credits both. It throws rather than returning a short map: a swallowed error here renders as "this team is clean".

## Customer-facing

The 86-entry admin registry was being pulled into the **golf calendar and tasks bundles** via `fetch-all-rows.ts → rls-denial.ts → feature-registry.ts`. Measured with esbuild, entry chunk: **42,556 B raw / 9,679 B gzipped → 1,912 B / 997 B**, registry moved to an async chunk the browser never requests.

## Failing toward reassurance

Several paths turned a broken read into a positive claim of health:

- `incident-feed.ts` destructured only `data`, so a PostgREST fault became `0 incidents` on the nav badge, KPI strip, triage queue and Errors tab at once.
- `briefing.ts` wrapped all seven checks in `catch { return null }` — and an empty list renders "All clear".
- `jobs.ts` computed `unreadableJobs` ("UNKNOWN, not never-ran") and the page never read it; unreadable jobs were counted **into** "All N cron jobs on schedule".
- `teams/[id]` never destructured `degraded`, so a failed error query rendered a green "No recent errors for this team" — on the page you open *because* you suspect that team has errors.
- Provider faults never reached the classifier branch built for them, so a spent Anthropic balance read as an app defect.
- Auto-resolve closed operator-gated provider faults on a deploy that had never rotated the credential.

## Feature health

Two RPC defects: the `p_features > 100` ceiling sat 15 short of the live registry behind a bare catch, and the heartbeat allowlist matched `golf\_%` only, so **no baseball feature could ever go amber** on a dead heartbeat.

Sizing that surfaced a bigger one: **18 of 43 baseball features named a heartbeat that could never resolve** — 15 pointing at a table that does not exist, 3 at a real table whose activity column isn't `created_at`. All repointed to the table each feature's *own* server actions write, counted from its action manifest rather than guessed from name similarity (the closest textual match for `baseball_lift_programs` was `baseball_program_settings`, which is wrong).

`baseball_lift_programs` turned out not to be an unapplied migration: production has **zero** `baseball_lift_*` tables and 33 `helm_lifting_*` ones, so re-running `20260624000063` would have created 20 dead tables. The family was superseded by the cross-sport lifting model.

## Migrations (both already applied and verified)

- `20260806030000` — ceiling 100 → 500, `baseball\_%` allowlisted
- `20260807020000` — optional `heartbeat_column`, `helm\_lifting\_%` allowlisted

Both verified live under a real super-admin JWT: `SECURITY DEFINER`/`STABLE`/`search_path` preserved, ACL unchanged (`service_role` was already granted), `anon` still blocked. Injection probes — bogus column, `id) FROM users--` in the column slot, non-allowlisted table — all resolve NULL without erroring.

**Expect ~15 baseball dots to turn amber.** They were green because the signal was missing, not because anything was healthy.

## Also

- A regression from `78c8cae9e` that never shipped: `AdminShell` hand-listed `['Operations','Apps','Platform']` while `ADMIN_NAV` had been regrouped — 10 of 17 tabs would have vanished from the rail, ⌘K and the phone More sheet under an empty heading. Now derived from `ADMIN_NAV`.
- `/admin/teams` and `/admin/billing` had one and zero inbound links respectively; nav now covers every route, test-guarded.
- Both double-fetches on `/admin` memoised. The feed wrapper takes a **primitive** because `cache()` keys on argument reference identity — two call sites passing their own `{windowHours: 24}` literal would have missed every time.
- Inngest is a truthful tri-state instead of `Boolean(env vars set)`; a dead key read "activated" for 10 days.
- Dark mode reaches `/admin`; `PanelBoundary` skeletons are compiler-enforced.

## Gates

fix(push): a device token that arrives before login is no longer thrown away

APNs/FCM delivers the device token exactly ONCE per launch, and on a cold
start it arrives while the app is still on the login screen. There is no
session, so registerDeviceToken answers UNAUTHORIZED_RETRYABLE — correctly.

The caller read that as a session-cookie propagation race and retried for
~15s (1s/2s/4s/8s backoff) before giving up. That can never succeed when
the truth is "nobody has signed in yet", and because APNs will not fire
`registration` again, the token was then dropped for the whole launch. The
device registered nothing and silently received no push, while the server
logged a warning that read like a benign race.

Measured on production for the week to 2026-08-06: of 7 registration
warnings, 6 were never followed by a device_tokens row.

The token is now parked instead of discarded, and submitted when a session
actually appears — CapacitorProvider flushes it on SIGNED_IN /
INITIAL_SESSION / TOKEN_REFRESHED. The short backoff is kept for the real
propagation race it was written for. A non-retryable rejection still drops
the token rather than re-attempting on every future auth event.

---

## How this was found, and how it was confirmed

Reported as `registerDeviceToken: Unauthorized` — 8 warnings in a week, and the code returns `UNAUTHORIZED_RETRYABLE` *by design* for a session-cookie race, so it reads as benign noise.

It isn't. Correlating each warning against a `device_tokens` row landing within 10 minutes:

| warning | token registered? |
|---|---|
| Aug 6 20:57 | **no** |
| Aug 5 01:43 | yes |
| Aug 3 14:21 | **no** |
| Aug 3 14:20 | **no** |
| Aug 3 14:20 | **no** |
| Aug 2 16:04 | **no** |
| Jul 31 14:13 | **no** |

**6 of 7 never landed.** Those devices got no push for the rest of the launch.

## Verification

- 8,998 tests passing (946 files) · typecheck 0 · lint 0 · `next build` exit 0
- 5 new tests covering the parked-token lifecycle: no-op flush, immediate success, **stays parked when unauthorized** (the actual fix), registers on later sign-in, and drops on a non-retryable rejection

## Note on scope

Two other bugs from the same sweep — coach-onboarding duplicate key and `addSecondTeam` RLS — turned out to be **already fixed** (18e6a7cf3 and 2bef266f0, both ancestors of the deployed commit). Their logged errors predate their fixes; `2bef266f0` was in fact prompted by the very occurrence I flagged. No changes made to either.

fix: today's production errors, at their roots

Swept every error source for the day — error_logs, admin_events,
admin_client_errors, background_job_logs, Postgres logs, Vercel runtime.
336 rows, of which most were `info`. Four real root causes:

1. Class sync was broken on EVERY re-sync of a saved class.
   golf_player_classes.start_time is a Postgres `time`, so PostgREST hands
   back "10:50:00" — and the sync appended ":00" to whatever it got,
   building "2026-06-01T10:50:00:00-04:00". Postgres rejected the batch.
   Three players hit it today; editing a saved class simply failed. Times
   are now normalized to HH:MM:SS once, up front, and an unparseable one
   is refused rather than silently becoming a midnight meeting.

2. AvatarUpload told a signed-in player they were signed out. It called
   getUser() — a NETWORK request — and destructured the error away, so a
   dropped request was indistinguishable from having no session. That
   request is at its most fragile in exactly the moment it runs: the OS
   photo picker has just handed control back and the radio is waking up.
   Hit a Shenandoah player mid-onboarding. Now reads the session the
   browser already holds, and distinguishes "can't check" from "expired".

3. The Bridge's team pages could never agree with its global feed.
   admin_events.team_id is populated on 0.5% of rows (7 of 1412 in a
   week) and on ZERO error-severity rows, so a team page read "no
   errors" while the feed showed 88 — UNC Wilmington's showed nothing at
   all. It also filtered on event_type and never on severity, and 906
   rows a week are event_type 'error' with severity 'info'. Fixing
   either alone makes it worse: attribution alone empties 906 routine
   "no rounds yet" rows onto the page as defects; severity alone leaves
   it blank. Both together take UNCW from 0 → 1 genuine error.

4. Two user-input rejections were filed as engineering defects. GoTrue's
   breach-corpus password rejection landed at 'error' while the app's own
   complexity rules — the same check — sat at 'info'. Same for a mistyped
   team code. Six rows a day of noise in the channel that was hiding (1).

Verified clean, not fixed because nothing was wrong: all 17 cron jobs
completed, admin_client_errors empty, Postgres errors were only my own
exploratory queries, and the single Vercel runtime group

## Summary

Follow-up to #1292. That fix stopped one player's classes from appearing on everyone else's calendar filter. The coach then asked the obvious next question — *"if I'm looking at a full calendar how do I know who is who?"*

He was right. Every class meeting rendered as the same neutral chip, with the owning player recorded nowhere on the row. On his own team, **Monday 11:30 has Braeden and Lucas in the same course with near-identical titles** — nothing distinguished them:

```
Mon 08-24 11:30   Business 332-001: Financial Management     ← Braeden
Mon 08-24 11:30   Integrative Experience 101: First Year     ← Kalani
Mon 08-24 11:30   BUS 332-001: Financial Management          ← Lucas
```

The `[class:<id>]` tag already links an event to its class, so this is display work — no migration.

- **Month chip** wears the owning player's identity tint — the same `tintFor(id)` their avatar uses in the member rail, on the roster, and in the attendee picker — plus their initials, because the palette is 8 wide and a roster can be larger. Tooltip names them outright.
- **Agenda / day / week card** gets a tinted `Braeden G.` pill beside the Class pill.
- **Detail drawer** shows the full name with an avatar dot, and stops printing the raw `[class:…]` marker under the instructor and credits.
- `class` added to the drawer's `TYPE_META` — a second copy of the card's map that was still saying "Event" for the same event the card called "Class".

## Also: visibility scoping (a judgment call worth reviewing)

Putting **names** on these blocks forces a question the previous PR didn't have to answer.

`golf_player_classes` RLS is explicit: a player may read their own classes, their coach may read the team's, a teammate may read neither. But the calendar showed every class to everyone, because they live in `golf_events`. Labelling them without fixing that would turn a quiet inconsistency into a published directory of the roster's whereabouts.

So: **a coach still sees the whole team** (that's the "All" lens he asked for), **a player now sees only their own.** RLS does most of the work — the owner index is fetched with the viewer's own client, so it arrives pre-scoped.

If you'd rather players keep seeing each other's classes, that's a one-line change in `attributeClassEvents`.

## Type of change

- [x] Bug fix
- [x] Feature / new behavior
- [ ] Security / RLS / auth
- [ ] Database migration
- [ ] CI / tooling / chore
- [ ] Docs only

## Area

golf · dashboard

## Risk level

- [ ] Low
- [x] Medium — changes what a player sees on the shared calendar; no schema or data change
- [ ] High

## Git Activity Timeline note

Class blocks on the team calendar now show which player they belong to, color-coded to match that player's avatar.

## Checklist

- [x] `npm run lint` and `npm run typecheck` pass locally (0 errors)
- [x] Unit tests pass — **8,983 passing, 944 files**; 11 new (8 attribution-logic, 3 render)
- [x] No migrations
- [x] RLS: no policy changes. The new owner lookup runs on the viewer's session client, so `golf_player_classes` RLS scopes it before the app sees it
- [x] No secrets
- [x] UI uses existing primitives — `StatusPill`, the established `tintFor` identity palette, existing chip geometry
- [x] Partner-readable summary + timeline note included

## Screenshots / notes

### Two details worth a reviewer's eye

**Attribution runs on the client-merged pages, not just the server payload.** Scrolling to another month fetches straight from `golf_events` via the browser client, and those rows arrive with no owner — attributing only server-side would leave a scrolled-to month unlabelled (and, for a player, leaking teammates' classes there). The pass is pure and idempotent, so it runs in both places.

**A failed owner lookup is "unknown", never "owns nothing".** Collapsing those two would make a player's own classes vanish from their calendar on a transient DB error. `classOwnersResolved` carries the distinction and is test-guarded.

### Deploy note

Not urgent — the fix the coach actually reported is already live. This is the enhancement on top.

body:
## Summary

A coach reported that filtering the golf calendar to his own avatar showed his whole roster's classes.

**Root cause:** class meetings *are* team events at the table level. `syncClassToCalendar` writes one `golf_events` row per class meeting onto the team calendar — deliberately, that's what puts classes on the calendar's "All" lens — but nothing on the row said whose class it was. `event_type` was `'other'` and the only owner link was a `[class:<id>]` tag buried in `description`. So every query that swept `golf_events` by `team_id` and called the result "someone's schedule" was wrong. On the reporting team that meant **578 upcoming "team events", 556 of which were two players' fall semesters.**

Two markers now carry the distinction (`src/lib/calendar/class-events.ts`):

| marker | means |
|---|---|
| `event_type = 'class'` | not a team event — filterable in SQL (`text NOT NULL`, so `.neq()` can't silently drop rows) |
| `description [class:<id>]` | whose class it is |

**Ownership.** `getUserBusyPeriods` splits the team sweep and resolves each class occurrence's owner against `golf_player_classes`, keeping only the caller's own. Fail-closed — an unresolvable tag (deleted class, unreadable under RLS) blocks nobody. A coach has no player row, so no class is ever theirs. This also fixes teammates' classes leaking into each other's availability and into event-conflict detection.

**Team-scoped reads now say "team events only":** coach dashboard count + calendar list, player dashboard today/upcoming, both iCal feeds, `get_coach_today_schedule`, and the CoachHelm chat calendar tool + program pulse. The last two are `LIMIT`-capped, so classes were crowding real events out of what the AI told the coach.

**`expandRecurringClass`** (the availability fallback for a class with no synced rows) compared full weekday names against the short codes actually stored (`'M'`, `'Th'`) and so had *never* produced anything. Fixed — but it has to stay bounded or a weekly rule marks a player busy forever, including over the summer. It's now bounded by the class's term, refuses to expand when the term is unknown, and skips classes that already have synced rows. `semester` is now persisted on class create/update/import; it was collected by the form and dropped on the floor, which is why every row was NULL.

Classes still appear on the calendar's "All" lens, now labelled **Class** instead of an unexplained "Event" chip.

## Partner-readable summary

A coach uploaded his players' class schedules from screenshots — that worked. But when he filtered the calendar to *his* calendar, he saw every player's classes, and his dashboard said he had 578 upcoming events when the team had 22. Classes were being stored as team events with no record of who they belonged to, so anything that asked "what's on this person's schedule?" answered with the whole roster's. Classes now belong to the player who owns them: they still show on the shared team calendar (coaches want that, and they're now labelled "Class"), they show on that specific player's schedule, and they stay off everyone else's — including the coach's. The same fix stops one player's semester from filling up the coach's dashboard, the team's subscribed calendar feed, and what CoachHelm reports as the week ahead.

## Type of change

- [x] Bug fix
- [ ] Feature / new behavior
- [ ] Security / RLS / auth
- [x] Database migration
- [ ] CI / tooling / chore
- [ ] Docs only

## Area

golf · dashboard · coachhelm

## Risk level

- [ ] Low
- [ ] Medium
- [x] High — includes a production data migration (666 rows) and a `SECURITY DEFINER` RPC replacement

## Git Activity Timeline note

Class schedules uploaded by players no longer appear on every teammate's and the coach's own calendar, dashboard, and calendar feed — they now belong to the player who owns them.

## Checklist

- [x] `npm run lint` and `npm run typecheck` pass locally (0 errors)
- [x] Unit/contract tests pass — 8,973 passing, 943 files; 8 new tests across `availability.test.ts`, `calendar-sync.test.ts`, `dashboard-data.test.ts`, `feed-window.test.ts`
- [x] **Migrations** reviewed for shared golf-prod safety — see migration notes below. No `DELETE`/`DROP TABLE`; one idempotent single-column `UPDATE` that guards its own reversibility precondition
- [x] **RLS:** no new tables. The new `golf_player_classes` ownership lookup was verified by role impersonation as the real coach (reads all 4 of the player's class rows via `golf_player_classes_select_team`) with an out-of-org control coach seeing 0
- [x] **No secrets** in the diff
- [x] UI change is two entries in existing token-based maps (`TYPE_META`, `TYPE_DOT_CLASS`) — a "Class" chip where an "Event" chip was
- [x] Partner-readable summary + timeline note included

## Screenshots / notes

### Migration plan — both already applied to production

Reviewed by `db-migration-reviewer` before applying. It surfaced one thing that changed how I applied it:

**`golf_events` is in the `supabase_realtime` publication**, and `use-calendar-range-events.ts` calls `router.refresh()` per message with no coalescing — so a single 666-row `UPDATE` would have fanned out one realtime message per row to every open calendar. The backfill was therefore applied **in batches of 100–150** rather than one statement. The migration file itself is idempotent and re-runs as a no-op.

The reviewer also flagged that the event-reminders cron might be emailing players about teammates' classes. **It isn't** — recipients derive from `golf_event_attendance`, and class events have zero attendance rows (verified). No change made there.

- `20260806020000_type_class_calendar_events.sql` — backfills class-tagged rows to `event_type = 'class'`. Idempotent. Raises rather than proceeding if any tagged row carries a third `event_type`, so the documented inverse stays exactly true:
  ```sql
  UPDATE golf_events SET event_type = 'other'
   WHERE event_type = 'class' AND description LIKE '%[class:%';
  ```
- `20260806020100_coach_today_schedule_excludes_classes.sql` — `CREATE OR REPLACE` of `get_coach_today_schedule` adding exactly one predicate (`event_type <> 'class'`); its `LIMIT 10` was filling with classes and pushing practice off the card. Authorization check, `SECURITY DEFINER`, `search_path`, jsonb shape and RSVP counts preserved verbatim. Grants re-asserted (`authenticated`, `service_role`; no `PUBLIC`/`anon`) and the `COMMENT` refreshed.

No broken window in either direction: pre-deploy the old UI renders class rows exactly as it does today (`typeMeta` already falls back), and post-deploy the code checks both markers.

### Verified on production data (Guilford College Men's Golf — the reporting team)

| | before | after |
|---|---:|---:|
| Coach's own calendar filter (busy blocks, 30d) | 48 | 22 |
| The owning player's own filter | 22 team + 26 classes | unchanged |
| Coach dashboard "Upcoming events" | 578 | 22 |
| Backfill | — | 666 typed, 0 missed, 0 non-class rows touched |

### Follow-up worth doing separately

`use-calendar-range-events.ts` fires a full `router.refresh()` per realtime message with no debounce. Adding one would de-risk every future bulk write to `golf_events`. Not done here — it wouldn't have been deployed at apply time anyway.

Three defects that made the Bridge read as stale, all found against live production data.

**1. `incident-feed.ts` — false "Regressed" badges.** `queryPriorResolutions` treated any prior resolution as a human fix, so a badge claimed "a fix failed." But `auto-resolve.ts:76` deliberately leaves `resolved_by` NULL on cron sweeps. All seven resolutions behind the badged rows were cron sweeps — 100% false positives. Now filtered with `.not('resolved_by', 'is', null)`.

**2. `activity.ts` — closed incidents replayed as live.** `fetchError()` had no `resolved` filter, so 281 already-resolved rows streamed into the activity feed as if happening now. That is most of why the feed read as stale.

**3. `triage.ts` — the queue led with the wrong thing.** Ranking was `affectedUsers DESC, lastSeen DESC`, but in production `affectedUsers` is nearly binary (seven groups with 1 user, ten with 0), so it decided almost nothing and recency arbitrated from second place where it could never outrank a stale 1-user row. The top item was 8.1 hours silent while two incidents from the last 18 minutes sat at #8 and #9. Liveness bands now lead; headcount still breaks ties *within* a band, preserving the original property that raw volume never ranks.

`livenessBand` takes `nowMs` as a parameter — calling `Date.now()` inside a comparator is a non-transitive sort.

Tests: `src/lib/admin/__tests__/triage-liveness-rank.test.ts`, 11 cases built on the real production shape.

Two things Shenandoah needs before inviting their staff.

## 1. The invite **link** now matches the squad

The labelled codes shipped earlier removed the ambiguity one level up — but the "Invite link" field underneath still only ever rendered the **active** team's URL. A coach who hit "Copy invite link" while viewing Men's sent the men's link regardless of who it was for. Exactly the trap the codes just closed.

Each squad row now carries its own **Copy link** beside its **Copy code**, and the single shared link field + button are hidden for two-squad programs. Single-team programs are unchanged — they have nothing to confuse. Regenerate is now explicit about which squad it affects.

## 2. Staff can join an **existing** program

Signing up as a coach always ran new-program onboarding, which creates an organization *and* a team. A coach entering Shenandoah's code would have created a **second Shenandoah** — the school duplicated, the real teams untouched, and nothing to signal it from the outside.

The role picker now offers **Player / Coach / Administrator**, and a coach or administrator who signs up with a program's code is attached to that program:

| role | staff rows | access | toggle |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Coach** | `assistant_coach` on the one team whose code they used | full access to that squad | no |
| **Administrator** | `head_coach` on **every** team in the org | both squads | **yes** |

This falls out of the existing model with **no policy changes and no new roles**. `is_golf_team_coach()` only asks whether a staff row exists, not which role it holds — so an assistant coach already has full team access. And `canSwitch = isHeadCoach && staffedTeams > 1` is exactly why a single-team coach sees no toggle while an admin does.

`admin` isn't an auth role either: at the auth layer they're a coach, and the program-head part is purely which staff rows get written.

### Guard rails

- refuses a code whose team has no organization
- refuses when the account already belongs to a **different** program — silently moving them would strip their old team's access
- skips teams they already staff, so a re-run can't duplicate rows
- **never** creates an organization

## Registry

`joinProgramAsStaff` registered under `join_team_flow`; both action-count tripwires bumped (433→434, 427→428) with the reason recorded inline.

Shenandoah's head coach could not add their Women's team **at all**. "Add team" → Women's → Create team returned *"Failed to create team. Please try again."* every time, so the program stayed on one team and the top-bar team toggle — which only renders for a head coach with more than one team — never appeared. That's the "he can't find the toggle" report.

## Root cause

From the production error log:

```
code=42501 msg=new row violates row-level security policy for table "golf_teams"
```

`.insert().select()` compiles to `INSERT ... RETURNING`, and **RETURNING is filtered by the SELECT policy**. `golf_teams_select` is `USING (is_golf_team_coach(id) OR is_golf_team_player(id))`, and `is_golf_team_coach` requires a `golf_team_coach_staff` row — which for a team being created *right now* does not exist yet; it's inserted moments later by the same action.

So the creator could never read back the team they had just made.

## Reproduced against production, isolating RETURNING from the write

| statement | result |
|---|---|
| `INSERT ... RETURNING` | **42501** |
| `INSERT` (no RETURNING) | succeeds |
| then `SELECT` as the creator | **0 rows** — the policy, as designed |
| then `SELECT` as admin | 1 row |

## Scope

Same defect in **all three** create paths — `addSecondTeam`, `createTeam`, and coach onboarding's Step 3 — so this was never about second teams specifically.

Each now inserts **without** a RETURNING and reads the row back with the admin client, scoped to the join code it just generated (unique). The INSERT still goes through the caller's client, so **the RLS write check still authorizes the create**; only the read-back is elevated, and the existing org-ownership assertion before the privileged staff insert is unchanged.

## Tests pin the shape, not the symptom

They fail if anyone chains `select()` onto the `golf_teams` insert again, and they assert the insert still uses the **caller's** client — so nobody "fixes" this later by doing the whole create as service-role and quietly dropping the write check. **4 of the 5 fail against the pre-fix code.**

`program-onboarding.test.ts` seeded `golf_teams` only on the user mock; the read-back is now on the admin client, so those seeds were mirrored.

#1278 added `assertGolfDemoWritable` but **nothing adopted it**, so merging it changed no behaviour. This wires it in — which is what actually protects a demo night.

## Why now

Every prospect entering the public golf demo signs into the **same** Supabase account, and that account shares an organization *and a team* with `njrini99@gmail.com` — Demo University Golf, 7 players, 12 events.

So an unguarded write is visible to every other concurrent visitor **and edits the owner's own team**. With a batch of coaches touring at once, the third one sees whatever the first one changed.

## Enforced at the wrapper, not in 49 function bodies

`withAdminObserved` gains a `demoSafe` flag. Every golf action already routes through it, so a mutation is marked declaratively next to its identity:

```ts
withAdminObserved('deleteGolfEvent', { sport: 'golf', demoSafe: true }, impl)
```

The alternative was a hand-edited assertion inside every mutating action, where the one that gets missed is the one that matters. **Reads are deliberately not marked** — guarding a read would break the tour itself.

Marked: team create/update/**regenerate-join-code**/accept+reject join request · roster removal · events · recurring events · qualifiers · announcements · tasks, templates + reminders · documents · travel itineraries + expenses · attendance.

Highest-consequence first: `regenerateJoinCode` would have let any prospect invalidate a real team's invite link.

## Resolves the session once, and fails OPEN for real users

The guard module fails **closed** on an unresolvable session. Called naively that means a transient GoTrue blip tells a paying coach they're "in a read-only demo" and refuses to save their work.

So the wrapper resolves the email through the existing `resolveObservedUser()` — which swallows errors and yields `null` — and hands it to the guard. An unresolvable session is then simply *not the demo account*, and the action's own auth check rejects it with the correct message.

The refusal is expected control flow: excluded from the wrapper's error reporting, and added to `instrumentation.ts`'s Sentry ignore list beside `BaseballDemoReadOnlyError` — otherwise a busy demo night arrives as dozens of "errors" that are the feature working.

## One existing test legitimately broke

`travel.test.ts` asserted "unauthorized when no user" with `mockReturnValueOnce`. A `demoSafe` action now reads auth twice — guard, then implementation — so the one-shot mock was consumed by the first and the second saw the signed-in default. **The action reported success for an unauthenticated caller.** Changed to a persistent value, which is what the scenario actually describes; `beforeEach` restores the default.

## Gates

- The two guard-specific assertions **fail against the unguarded wrapper**, pass with it

Three things in the admin surface.

## 1. Zero routes into the retired `/golf/admin` console

Backing out of the Coach CRM dropped you on the old GolfHelm console instead of Helm Bridge. Every door is now closed:

- **`next.config.mjs`** redirects `/golf/admin` → `/admin`. **Exact path only** — `/golf/admin/crm` and `/golf/admin/demo-sessions` are still live and are *not* part of the rule. Verified by request rather than by reading the regex:

| request | result |
|---|---|
| `/golf/admin` | **307 → `/admin`** |
| `/golf/admin/crm` | normal auth bounce, `returnTo` intact |
| `/golf/admin/demo-sessions` | normal auth bounce, `returnTo` intact |

  Temporary (307), not permanent — a 308 is cached hard by browsers and this is a product decision that may be revisited. The old `page.tsx` stays in the tree, so reverting is one line.

- **`resolveAdminPostLoginPath()`** now returns `/admin`. Five call sites inherit it (login action, dashboard layout, welcome, login bounce, native cold-start).
- The CRM's two back affordances and three error-boundary `homePath`s point at `/admin`; the sidebar label reads **Helm Bridge**.

### Lockout check before changing the resolver

`/admin` is gated by `SUPER_ADMIN_USER_IDS`, which is encrypted in Vercel and unreadable. Production has exactly **one** `users.role='admin'` account (`admin@helmsportslabs.com`), so pointing the resolver at `/admin` could in principle have locked it out.

Resolved behaviourally: signed in on production and observed that **login already lands on `/admin`** and Helm Bridge serves it. That account is already a super-admin. Documented in `admin-redirect.ts`, including what to do if a future `role='admin'` account is *not* added to the allowlist.

## 2. Deliverability status chips were unreadable

Dark-green text on a dark-green fill. They were `<Button variant="primary">`, and only one is ever selected — so the six unselected chips each kept the primary variant's solid accent fill while the unselected branch of the `className` ternary set only a text colour, never a background. The selected chip looked fine purely because `bg-nav-bg` happened to override the fill.

Now `variant="ghost"` with explicit `bg-transparent` on the unselected branch, plus `role="group"` and `aria-pressed`, which these chips never had.

Swept the rest of the admin tree for the same shape — `SegmentBadge`'s chip variant sets its own background and its pill variant is already ghost. **This was the only instance.**

## 3. The Cup of Helm digest now logs *where* it went

Reported as "it said delivered and it never was". It **had** been delivered — to `njrini99@gmail.com`, on time, every day. Resend confirms `email.delivered`; the admin alias simply is not on `OPS_DIGEST_TO`, despite `transport.ts`'s own comment saying the briefing goes to "the admin alias AND a personal address".

The job log couldn't answer that question: it recorded `{ sent: true }` and nothing else, which cannot distinguish "never sent" from "sent somewhere you weren't looking". `sendOpsAlert` now returns the recipient list alongside the message id, and the cron records both.

**The env var is unchanged** — which inboxes receive the briefing is the owner's call.

- eslint 0 errors
- 8876/8876 unit tests pass
- `next build` exit 0

Chip contrast is asserted on production after deploy — the Resend view has no data locally.

High severity

  • GHSA-m8rv-5g2x-5cg5: a malicious type property on a duck-typed blob-like HTTP/1.1 request body could inject CRLF sequences into the generated content-type header. Undici now coerces and validates the value before adding it to the request. Fixed by 33928bc2.

body:
Follow-up to #1279. Found by querying the `notifications` table after a real end-to-end join on production, rather than trusting the join's own return value — the join succeeded and the player landed on the roster, but **no notification was written**. The most recent `team_join` notification in production is **2026-02-10**.

## Two independent causes

Both silent, because the block is wrapped in a best-effort `try/catch` so a notification can never fail a join.

1. **#1279** fixed the team lookup feeding the message — it ran *before* the membership INSERT, so it was RLS-denied, `team` was null, and the whole block was skipped. Necessary but **not sufficient**.
2. `notifications_insert_own` is `WITH CHECK (user_id = auth.uid())`. The insert ran as the joining **player** and addressed rows to the **coach**, so Postgres rejected every row. No client-side change could satisfy that policy.

```
notifications_insert_own | INSERT | with_check: (user_id = ( SELECT auth.uid() ))
```

## Fix

The insert now uses the service-role client, matching the CoachHelm dispatcher's in-app receipt (`lib/coachhelm/v3/notifications/dispatch.ts`).

Elevating is appropriate here: the join was already authorized by `golf_join_team_with_code`, the recipients are exactly the coaches of the org that owns the joined team, and every field of the payload is server-derived. The insert's error is now **logged instead of discarded**, so the next such failure is visible rather than silent.

## Tests

Assert the notification goes through the **service-role** client specifically — a regression to the caller's client would be silently dropped by RLS while the join still reports success, which is precisely how this survived six months. Against the pre-fix code the two new assertions fail.

Also pinned: no notification is sent when the join itself failed.

- eslint 0 errors
- **8876/8876** unit tests pass
